stops.name: Berlin, solo evening at the Bachsaal
stops.campa: On an autumn evening she dances at the Bachsaal on the Lützowstraße, the concert hall of the Klindworth-Scharwenka conservatory, one of the consecrated rooms of the Berlin solo dance. The celebrated soloist of the congresses gives the capital her cycle of abstract dances: arms circling in machine-time, the thrust, the strike, the turn, the monotonous form repeated until it opens. The critics have learned her category by now and write it as she taught them to: not expression-dance but abstrakter Tanz, a thing with laws, danced by its lawgiver.

stops.name: Berlin, the two essays on Wigman
stops.campa: In 1930 she publishes her double portrait of the teacher: Mary Wigmans Führertum and Mary Wigmans Kompositionsstil, Wigman's leadership, Wigman's style of composition. The first pupil measures the founder with a compass, honoring the priestess by analyzing the rite. It is the abstract dancer's homage: not adoration but anatomy, the ecstatic school described in the cool grammar of form. The Dresden gods are given their exact due by the one heretic they raised themselves, and the essays enter the permanent scripture of the movement.

stops.name: Munich, the third Dancers' Congress, with her students
stops.campa: June 1930: the third and last of the great congresses, at Munich. Skoronel comes now not only as the famous soloist but as a head of school, her students around her, the abstract method embodied in a generation she has trained from the first exercise. The congress quarrels, as congresses do, over theater and freedom, Laban and Wigman, bread and art; she stands in it as the proof that a doctrine can be taught. It is her last synod. The movement has four more summers; she has not quite two.

stops.name: Berlin-Wilmersdorf, the students: Charlotte Bara comes to the school
stops.campa: Through the halls of the Blüthgenstraße pass the bodies that will carry her out into the century: Hanna Berger, Ilse Meudtner, Lisa Czóbel who will dance in the premiere of The Green Table, Oda Schottmüller who will die under the executioner as a resister, and from the south comes Charlotte Bara, the Gothic dancer of Ascona, who takes her training with Trümpy and Skoronel in Berlin and bears the method back to the Teatro San Materno above the lake, where the holy mountain of Laban's youth keeps its own theater.

stops.name: Berlin, the Dante inscribed: alles, alles Gute
stops.campa: On the first of February 1931 she takes a volume of Dante's Divine Comedy in Stefan George's translation, the sternest German ever made of the poem of the other world, and writes a farewell in it for a departing student of the school, wishing her everything, everything good, and signs and dates the page. The book survives her; the dealers keep it under glass. In this register the relic reads itself: the dying dancer's hand, Dante's journey through the dark, and a blessing given twice over.
stops.quote: Ich wünsche Ihnen alles, alles Gute. Vera Skoronel, 1. Feb. 1931
stops.quote_source: Autograph dedication in Dante, Göttliche Komödie, trans. Stefan George, copy from the Trümpy-Schule, Berlin (antiquarian record, Librairie du Cardinal)

stops.name: Berlin-Wilmersdorf, the sickness in the blood
stops.campa: The blood itself turns against the fastest body in Berlin. Through 1931 the sickness the chronicles call a Blutkrankheit wears her down; those near her speak of chronic exhaustion, of a woman enchanting and madly gifted who disturbs every communal peace and cannot spare herself, who teaches and composes against the failing of her own instrument. The name given in the nursery keeps its second edge now: skoro, quickly, soon. She does not stop working. The abstract dance was always a discipline against the body's nature; she holds the discipline.

stops.name: Berlin, death of Vera Skoronel
stops.campa: On the 24th of March 1932, in Berlin, Vera Skoronel dies of the disease of the blood. She is twenty-five years old. The Weimar dance loses its severest architect ten months before the Republic itself begins to die; she is spared the sight of the movement she helped build being marched into step by the coming state. The canon closes her ledger cleanly: one Evil Square, one Split Man, one Awakening of the Masses, one Tanzspiel, one doctrine of the abstract dance, one school full of students. Twenty-five years.

stops.name: Berlin, Fritz Cremer casts the right hand
stops.campa: At the deathbed the young sculptor Fritz Cremer takes plaster and casts her right hand: the hand that drew the ghostly colored-pencil figures, that wrote the doctrine of the abstract dance, that cut counter-rhythms through the air of the Blüthgenstraße studio. The gesture belongs to the old rite of the death mask, but what is kept of the dancer is not the face: it is the instrument. The cast survives as her one bodily relic: the fastest hand in the German dance, stopped and made permanent at twenty-five.

stops.name: Berlin, burial in the Friedhof Wilmersdorf
stops.campa: They bury her in the cemetery of Wilmersdorf, the borough of her school, a short walk from the house Gellhorn built for the abstract dance. Trümpy, the friend and other half of the pact, survives her by fifty-one years and carries the school on alone before merging it away; the grave stays in the quarter where the work was done. The dancers of Berlin lay the fastest of their number into the slowest of all figures, the ground, and the name on the stone is the childhood cry: quickly.

stops.name: Berlin, the name dances again: Tanztheater Skoronel
stops.campa: Fifty-two years after the burial, in West Berlin, the choreographer Judith Kuckart founds a free dance-theater company and gives it the dead girl's name: Tanztheater Skoronel. The papers meanwhile gather in Cologne, at the German Dance Archive, brought by the brother Boris and out of Trümpy's estate: the drawings, the manuscripts on the abstract dance, the photographs by Lotte Jacobi. The canon's verdict stands as Toepfer writes it: no dancer of the Weimar era pursued the modernist group form more fiercely. The name keeps its promise: Vera, quickly, again.
